conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospital doctors. You’re here because of abdominal pain. Can you tell me about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… it’s the same pain I always get. Right here, in the middle, above my belly button. It’s been getting worse over two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And have you been nauseous or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a lot. I haven’t been able to keep food down. I’ve also had loose stools sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers, chest pain, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that. Just the pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your labs show a slightly high lipase, but your liver tests, kidney function, and blood count are normal. That means we don’t think this is pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve had this before. They said it might be pancreatitis or something with my gallbladder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know your history. You’ve had many tests—ERCPs, MRIs, CT scans—all normal. A HIDA scan recently showed your gallbladder ejection fraction was about 55%, which is a bit low but not low enough to say it’s the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, we think it’s an episode of acute pain on top of your chronic condition. It could be related to gut motility or functional pain. We’re not seeing any surgical issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had gallstones before, though. Could that be it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have had gallstones in the past, but your recent specialist review didn’t think cholecystectomy would help. The pain pattern doesn’t match typical gallbladder disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. I just want it to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help with that. For now, you’ll stay NPO—nothing by mouth—for a few hours to rest your stomach. We’ll give IV fluids and medications for pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The pain is still there, but not as intense. I haven’t vomited since I got here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We’re going to start you on clear liquids—water, broth, apple juice. If you tolerate that, we’ll move to soft food tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have tea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, plain tea is fine. No milk or cream. We’ll go slow to make sure your stomach can handle it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well with clear liquids. Any nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a little, but not bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll switch you to a soft diet—things like mashed potatoes, applesauce, toast. And we’re changing your pain meds from IV to oral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I won’t need the IV anymore?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the IV for fluids a bit longer, but you’re moving in the right direction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You slept well? Any pain overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did okay. Took the hydromorphone once. Woke up with some pain, but it settled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your vitals are stable. We’re going to advance your diet to regular food today if you’re up for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s great. I miss real food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but take it slow. Small portions. Let us know if you feel nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You ate lunch and kept it down. That’s excellent progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel much better. The pain is mild now, mostly with pressing on my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your exam shows mild tenderness, but no signs of infection or blockage. We’re confident this is not a surgical issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my other medicines? I take several for anxiety and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued your venlafaxine, clonazepam, imipramine, and prazosin. They’re important for your mental health and may even help with pain regulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I get anxious when I’m in pain and can’t sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. Your mental health is part of your care. We’ll make sure you have your meds when you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. You’re on regular food, pain is mild, and you’re not needing much medication. We’re thinking you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But what if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send you home with acetaminophen and a small amount of hydromorphone for breakthrough pain. Also prochlorperazine for nausea if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your gastroenterologist this week. They’ll help manage your chronic pain and decide if any further testing is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been in so many times. I just want to avoid this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know it’s been hard. The goal is to manage flare-ups at home when possible. But you did the right thing coming in when you couldn’t eat or keep things down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re finalizing your discharge. You’re doing well—eating, pain controlled, no nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Thank you for helping me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take your meds as prescribed. Use the hydromorphone only if needed, and don’t hesitate to call your doctor if symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I have my follow-up appointment already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be out by midday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave. Any pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a little soreness, nothing bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your exam looks good. Soft belly, normal bowel sounds. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Rest, stay hydrated, and follow up. We’re here if you need us.
